texts: Aelmere is a village on the northern coast.
Aelmere sits at the head of a horseshoe inlet.
good. Aelmere keeps its name and its village type, and "on the northern coast" is recorded as a position relation onto a typed coast, with nothing invented.
good. the position clause reads cleanly: Aelmere sits in the head, the head is part of the inlet, and "horseshoe inlet" keeps its own kind with "inlet" as its genus.
good. the grey cliffs come out as one specific set that surrounds the inlet, with "grey" handed to each cliff by a rule that fires as soon as any individual cliff is named.
good. "many stone houses" becomes a counted group of stone houses that Aelmere holds, and "many" is recorded as a vague count rather than silently turned into a number.
good. the houses are one specific group, and "have slate roofs" is recorded both of the group and, by a rule, of each house individually.
good. "Cauldron Hall" becomes a named individual whose hall type is read off the name itself, located in Aelmere — this is the shape to copy for other named buildings.

mixed: the location is recorded correctly, but "The Watch" is read as an ordinary noun (a watch), so it lands as an anonymous unnamed thing — unlike "Cauldron Hall" one line above, nothing later in the world can point back to it. Stating the kind in a separate word is what signals that Watch is a name: "The Watch, a tower, stands in Aelmere." (substitute the true kind — tower, hall, keep — for "tower").
The Cliff Path runs along the outer edge of the village.
The Cliff Path runs from the harbor wall to the cliff-spires.
The cliff-spires stand east of the village.
Flat sea-worn stones pave the Cliff Path.
Each Keeper walks the Cliff Path every night.
The Cliff Path holds one hundred and twelve lanterns.
The middle stretch of the Cliff Path is unshielded.

(: stones_pave_path (Implication (And (Member $x stone) (Member $x flat) (Member $x sea_worn)) (And (Member (sk_pave $x) pave) (Agent (sk_pave $x) $x) (Patient (sk_pave $x) cliff_path))) (STV 0.9 0.9))

(: keeper_walk_rule (Implication (Member $x keeper) (And (Member (sk_walk $x) walk) (Agent (sk_walk $x) $x) (Theme (sk_walk $x) cliff_path) (Time (sk_walk $x) night) (Every (sk_walk $x) 1 day))) (STV 1.0 0.9))

mixed: the path-along-the-outer-edge relation is recorded correctly, but "the village" lands as an anonymous unnamed village that is never tied to Aelmere, so this fact never joins the rest of the world. If the village is Aelmere, name it: "The Cliff Path runs along the outer edge of Aelmere."

good. the path keeps its name and its path type, and both termini are kept as from-the-harbor-wall and to-the-cliff-spires relations on the path itself (the verb "runs" carries nothing of its own, as in any stands/sits/runs position clause).

mixed: "east of" is recorded correctly, but "the village" again lands as an anonymous unnamed village, so the sentence anchors the spires to nothing that appears anywhere else. Write: "The cliff-spires stand east of Aelmere."

bad: the bare plural "Flat sea-worn stones" was read as a claim about stones in general, so the parse became a rule saying that every flat, sea-worn stone anywhere paves the Cliff Path — and the actual set of stones surfacing this one path never appears. Make the set specific: "The stones that pave the Cliff Path are flat and sea-worn." (the passive "The Cliff Path is paved with flat, sea-worn stones." works too).
good. "Each Keeper" becomes a rule giving every Keeper a nightly walk of the Cliff Path, with the night slot and the daily cycle both recorded; it fires as soon as a Keeper is named.
good. one hundred and twelve is recorded as an exact count on the lantern group the named path holds.
good. the middle stretch is recorded as a part of the Cliff Path, carrying "unshielded" as a positive property of its own.
The harbor wall holds twenty-four lanterns.
The fishing boats use the harbor lanterns as beacons at night.
The harbor lanterns are short and squat.
Whenever wind reflects off the water at the harbor wall, a harbor lantern burns its mire-essence quickly.
Harbor-lantern Keepers live near the harbor.

(: l16_boats_rule (Implication (PartOf $x sk_boats_1) (And (Member (sk_use $x) use) (Agent (sk_use $x) $x) (Theme (sk_use $x) sk_lanterns_1) (As (sk_use $x) beacon) (Time (sk_use $x) night))) (STV 1.0 0.9))

(: whenever_reflect_burn (Implication (And (Member $e reflect) (Patient $e wind) (Off $e sk_water_1)) (And (Member (sk_burn $e) burn) (Agent (sk_burn $e) sk_lantern_1) (Patient (sk_burn $e) sk_essence_1) (Manner (sk_burn $e) quickly) (During (sk_burn $e) $e))) (STV 1.0 0.9))
good. the wall is typed as a harbor wall (with "wall" as its genus) and holds a lantern group counted at twenty-four.

good. the boats, the lanterns, the beacon capacity and "at night" are all kept, and the use is recorded both of the boat group and of each individual boat, so a later fact about one boat still connects.
good. "short" and "squat" are each handed to every harbor lantern by their own rule, rather than being pinned on the group as a single object.

bad: in the result clause "a harbor lantern" was pinned to one particular lantern that the parse also asserts to exist outright, so the rule reads "that same single lantern burns its essence every time" instead of "whichever harbor lantern is involved, on each occasion". Use the definite plural, so the lanterns are the ones the world already established: "Whenever wind reflects off the water at the harbor wall, the harbor lanterns burn their mire-essence quickly." If you mean it lantern-by-lantern, put the lantern into the condition instead: "Whenever wind reflects off the water at a harbor lantern, that lantern burns its mire-essence quickly."
good. the bare plural becomes a fireable rule giving every harbor-lantern Keeper a lives-near-the-harbor fact, and the compound kind carries its own keeps-harbor-lanterns atoms.
The Sunken Cove lies west of the village.
The Cove Stair leads down to the Sunken Cove.
The Cove Stair is a narrow descending path.
A stone landing stands at the foot of the Cove Stair.
The landing extends into shallow water.
The bones of the old graveyard lie under the water of the Sunken Cove.
When the tide is low, the grave markers are visible below the surface.
The Sunken Cove is cold in every season.

(: t1_rule (Implication (And (Member $s low) (Experiencer $s sk_tide_1) (PartOf $x sk_group_1)) (And (Member (sk_visible $s $x) visible) (Experiencer (sk_visible $s $x) $x) (During (sk_visible $s $x) $s) (Below (sk_visible $s $x) sk_surface_1))) (STV 1.0 0.9))
good. the named cove, its kind, the village and the west-of relation are all carried, and the stative 'lies' correctly adds no event.

mixed: the connection and its endpoint are recorded, but 'down' is dropped entirely — the parse says only that the stair leads to the Cove, not that it goes downward. Put the direction in the verb, where it cannot be dropped: 'The Cove Stair descends to the Sunken Cove.'
good. the path kind and both modifiers are carried, and the two-word name stays one stable symbol.
good. the landing, the foot of the stair, the part-whole link and the position are all recorded.

mixed: the spatial relation survives, but the verb 'extends' is recorded nowhere and 'into' — a direction — is pressed into service as a static position head, so the parse says only that the landing is 'into' shallow water. Use a plain position clause with a containment preposition: 'The far end of the landing lies in shallow water.'
good. the graveyard and its age, the bones as a set, the cove's water and the 'under' relation are all carried, with no unstated part-whole links invented.

bad: the condition 'the tide is low' is a state rather than an event, so the translator has to invent an eventuality for the rule to hang its timing on, and the resulting rule stores only a reified visibility state — a plain 'is this marker visible?' binds nothing. Give the condition its own finite verb and make the consequent about each marker rather than a definite plural: 'Whenever the tide falls, each grave marker is visible below the surface.'
good. the cold state, the flat 'is cold' fact and the every-season recurrence are all carried.
The Stilllight Lantern stands at the top of the Cove Stair.
The Sunken Cove holds one lantern.
The Stilllight Lantern stands at the Sunken Cove.
The Stilllight Lantern is a large lantern.
Iron bands reinforce the Stilllight Lantern.
The Stilllight Lantern burns through a full night on one filling.
The Stilllight Keeper walks down the Cove Stair at midnight.
The Stilllight Keeper checks the flame at midnight.
The Stilllight station is a demanding station.
The Keepers fear the Stilllight station.
good. the lantern, the stair, the top-of-the-stair part and the position are all carried.

bad: the numeral 'one' is dropped — the parse is atom for atom what 'holds a lantern' would give, so the count is lost. A number only survives when it rides a set (as in 'There are seven pools'), and a singular noun gives it nowhere to land, so put the one-ness in a word that is recorded as a property: 'The Sunken Cove holds a single lantern.'
good. both names, both kinds and the containment position are carried.
good. the name, the lantern kind and the 'large' property are all carried, with 'large' kept separate rather than fused into the kind.

bad: 'Iron bands' as a bare plural reads as a claim about iron bands in general, so the parse became a rule saying that ANY iron band anywhere reinforces this lantern — something the sentence does not say. Make the bands definite so they become one specific set doing one reinforcing: 'The iron bands reinforce the Stilllight Lantern.'

mixed: the burning, a night's duration and the filling are recorded, but 'one' and 'full' are both dropped, so the endurance claim — a whole night on a single filling — is weakened to 'burns a night on a filling'. Split it into two claims that survive intact: 'The Stilllight Lantern burns from dusk to dawn. It is filled once a night.'

mixed: the keeper, the stair and midnight are all recorded, but 'down the Cove Stair' is folded into a plain location role, so the parse says the walking happened at the stair and the descent is lost. Put the direction in the verb: 'The Stilllight Keeper descends the Cove Stair at midnight.'
good. the keeper, the flame, the checking and the midnight time are all carried, and no recurrence is invented beyond what the sentence states.

mixed: the sentence's own content is carried, but 'the Stilllight station' (capitalised name plus lower-case common noun) is read here as a station belonging to a separate entity called Stilllight, while the same phrase in the next sentence is read as the named thing itself — so the two sentences end up about different objects. Capitalise the whole name so it is one stable symbol: 'The Stilllight Station is a demanding station.'

mixed: the fearing and its participants are recorded, but two labels lose content — 'the Keepers' becomes a bare name with no link to the keeper kind (nothing ties it to the Stilllight Keeper, or to keepers at all), and 'the Stilllight station' is read differently here than in the previous sentence. Write 'The keepers fear the Stilllight Station.' — the lower-case plural makes them a group of keepers, and the fully capitalised name keeps one symbol for the station.
The Salt-bloom Tide-pools lie north of the village.
A goat-path along the cliff top leads to the Salt-bloom Tide-pools.
The Salt-bloom Tide-pools are small pools in a stone shelf above the tide-line.
Two pools at the south end never bloom.
Whenever a spring tide comes, the tide-pools fill and overflow.
The Keepers visit the tide-pools at harvest time.
The Council surveys the tide-pools occasionally.

mixed: the north-of relation and the village are recorded correctly, but the plural name is stored as one individual typed as a single tide-pool, so the fact that the site is several pools has no carrier anywhere. Make the head a common-noun plural so the pools become a set attached to the named site: 'The Salt-bloom tide-pools lie north of the village.'

mixed: the goat-path, the cliff top and the destination are all carried; the only loss is the same one as the previous sentence — 'the Salt-bloom Tide-pools' is stored as one individual typed as a single pool. Lower-case the head noun: 'A goat-path along the cliff top leads to the Salt-bloom tide-pools.'

mixed: the stone shelf, the tide-line and both position relations are carried, but 'are small pools' collapses onto the single named individual, so the parse says the named thing is one small pool rather than that there are several small pools. Lower-case the head so the plural becomes a set the description can distribute over: 'The Salt-bloom tide-pools are small pools in a stone shelf above the tide-line.'
good. the set of pools and the exact count are both recorded.

good. the two pools, their count, their position at the south end and the never-blooming denial are all carried — the denial at both the group level and per pool, with 'never' recorded as the quantifier word.
good. the rule fires on any spring tide and both verbs get their own fireable rule, with the filling and overflowing tied to the tide that triggered them.

mixed: the visit, the pools and 'at harvest time' are all recorded, but 'the Keepers' becomes a bare name with no link to the keeper kind, so nothing ties these visitors to keepers or to the Stilllight Keeper. Use a lower-case plural so they are recorded as a group of keepers: 'The keepers visit the tide-pools at harvest time.'

bad: 'occasionally' has no home in the representation, so the translator discounted the whole clause to half true — the parse now says the Council is only half the surveyor and the pools only half the thing surveyed, which the sentence never claims. Move the vagueness into an adjective on the surveys, where it is recorded at full strength: 'The Council makes occasional surveys of the tide-pools.'
Cauldron Hall is a long low building near the harbor.
Cauldron Hall has thick walls of dark stone.
Cauldron Hall has a tall slate chimney.
Cauldron Hall holds three copper cauldrons.
Each cauldron sits on a stone hearth.
The Council appoints a Keeper as Cauldron Hall Warden each season.
Hesper is the current Cauldron Hall Warden.
Hesper is a careful and silent man.
good. the size adjectives stay separate properties of the hall instead of being fused into its kind, and "near the harbor" keeps the surface preposition attached to the building itself.

bad: "of dark stone" has no licensed encoding for what a thing is MADE of, so the parse fell back on the possessive link — which says each wall BELONGS TO the stone rather than being made of it — and the ruling was that the only compliant repair is to drop the material link entirely, losing "dark stone" altogether. Put the material in front of the head noun instead: "Cauldron Hall has thick dark stone walls." — "stone walls" then fuses into a kind of its own carrying the wall genus, and "thick" and "dark" are handed to each wall by the usual per-member rule.
good. "slate chimney" fuses into one kind carrying its chimney genus, "tall" stays a separate property, and nothing is invented for "has".

mixed: the parse is right apart from one extra atom, (Inheritance copper_cauldron copper), which reads "a copper cauldron is a kind of copper"; the ruling is simply to drop it, leaving "copper" inside the fused kind symbol where it is still recorded. Nothing in your wording caused this — "three copper cauldrons" is exactly the counted-group-plus-fused-kind shape the translator wants — so keep the sentence as it is.
good. "each" becomes a per-cauldron rule that fires for any cauldron and gives each one its own stone hearth, and "sits on" is recorded as a position with no event invented.

mixed: every atom is true, but two things do not survive — the "as Cauldron Hall Warden" designation has no encoding, so nothing links the appointing to the office (the warden atoms that are there rest on a construction the instruction set does not cover and may come out differently on a re-parse), and one Keeper witness stands for every season, so "a different Keeper each season" is not recoverable. Give the office its own finite clause: "Each season the Council appoints a Keeper. The Keeper is the Cauldron Hall Warden." The season-to-season change of person still has no carrier either way, so expect the Keeper to read as one standing person.

mixed: the one flagged atom, (Inheritance current_warden current), was struck — a rank adjective like "current" may never be exposed — which leaves "current" buried inside the fused symbol current_warden and no longer queryable. Move it out of the title and it becomes a proper time anchor instead: "Hesper is now the Cauldron Hall Warden."
good. "careful" and "silent" stay two separate properties of Hesper rather than fusing into the noun, which is what the instruction set wants for incidental character description.
The Watch is a small square stone hall in the center of the village.
The Watch holds the Council's ledger-room.
The Watch holds the village's feather store.
The feather store is a sealed bin in the floor of the ledger-room.
An iron lid closes the feather bin.
The Council holds keys to the feather bin.
The feather-collectors hold keys to the feather bin.
The Council sits at a long oak table in the Watch.
good. "stone hall" fuses into one kind carrying its hall genus while "small" and "square" stay separate properties, and "in the center of the village" comes out as two nested containment links.
good. the Council's ledger-room is attached by the loose-association possessive (a ledger-room is not a component of a council) and "ledger-room" keeps its room genus.
good. "feather store" fuses with its store genus, the village's claim on it is the same opaque possessive link, and nothing is added for the plain present tense.
good. "sealed bin" stays two atoms rather than one fused kind, "the floor of the ledger-room" is read as a genuine part of the room, and the store's position is recorded without inventing an event.
good. both compounds keep their head genus with the material word left inside the symbol, and the lid is the actor while the bin is what changes state.
good. the keys come out as a group with "to the feather bin" attached directly to them, and "the Council" stays one collective actor with no per-member claims invented.

good. the definite plural gets both a group-level holding and a per-collector rule, which is the sanctioned pairing — the reviewer's objection, that each collector's key is minted separately from the group's keys, was refuted on adjudication.

good. "oak table" fuses with its table genus, "long" stays a separate property, and both positions are recorded with no event invented; note that "in the Watch" was attached to the table rather than to the sitting, which comes to the same thing here.
The Hollows lie inland from the village.
The Hollows are a long stretch of low scrub forest.
The Hollows lanterns stand along the forest paths.
The Keepers keep the Hollows lanterns dim.
Whenever a nightmoth flees the Cliff Path, the nightmoth goes to a dim lantern in the Hollows.
A small crew of Keepers tends the Hollows.
The Hollows produce a thin thread harvest.
(: fog_cover (And (Member sk_cover_1 cover) (Agent sk_cover_1 fog) (Theme sk_cover_1 hollows)) (STV 0.8 0.9))

(: e2_rule (Implication (And (Member $m nightmoth) (Member $e flee) (Agent $e $m) (Theme $e cliff_path)) (And (Member (sk_go $e) go) (Agent (sk_go $e) $m) (Goal (sk_go $e) (sk_lantern $e)) (Member (sk_lantern $e) lantern) (Member (sk_lantern $e) dim) (LocatedIn (sk_lantern $e) hollows) (During (sk_go $e) $e))) (STV 1.0 0.9))
good. "lie" is kept as a position rather than turned into an event, and "inland from" is recorded as a single surface link from the Hollows to the village.

mixed: every atom is true, but "a long stretch of low scrub forest" has no encoding for the "stretch of" relation, so the of-phrase is flattened onto the Hollows and "low" ends up predicated of the Hollows rather than of the scrub forest it modifies. Drop the extent noun and let the adjectives sit on the thing itself: "The Hollows are a long low scrub forest."

mixed: the content is right but the shape is wrong — the habitual is packed into a single strength-0.8 bundle, the form reserved for denials, so it reads as one particular covering rather than as a regularity; the compliant form is a rule ("for any fog, it covers the Hollows") at that same 0.8. This one is our defect and not your wording, so no rewrite is called for — the same sentence re-parsed yields the right shape. One residual worth knowing: "usually" can only be carried as a strength on a rule about fog, never as "on most occasions", which is a limitation we have registered.
good. the count comes out as a group of thirty-two lanterns held by the Hollows, with no per-lantern claims invented.
good. each lantern gets its own "along the forest paths" position through a per-lantern rule, and "The Hollows lanterns" is tied to the Hollows by the loose-association possessive.
good. the group burns and each lantern separately burns as well, with "dimly" kept in its surface form as the manner.
good. "keep ... dim" comes out as a maintained state linked to the keeping, with a per-lantern rule giving each lantern its dimness; "the Keepers" is recorded as one named actor.

good. this is the shape worth imitating — one finite clause per event, the subject repeated explicitly instead of pronominalized, and "whenever" yielding a rule that fires for every nightmoth with its destination lantern minted per occurrence.
good. the crew is one collective actor, "small" is read as a property of the crew itself rather than of its members, and the members are typed as Keepers.
good. "thread harvest" fuses with its harvest genus while "thin" stays a separate property of the harvest.
The Northcove is a small cove.
The Northcove lies north of the village.
Two cliff-spires curve outward around the Northcove.
The cliff-spires shield the Northcove against the north wind.
The Northcove lanterns stand along a curving inner shore.
Northcove lanterns never go out in winter.
The Northcove is a reliable production-row.
good. the name, the cove kind and the size adjective each land as their own atom, so 'is the Northcove a cove?' and 'is it small?' both answer.
good. the position is recorded as a direct north-of link from the Northcove to a village referent, and no spurious event is minted for 'lies'.

mixed: the two spires, the count and the around-the-cove relation all land and the per-spire rule fires, but the directional adverb 'outward' has no slot in our translator and is silently dropped, so the outward flare of the spires goes unrecorded. If that direction matters, give it its own finite clause: "Two cliff-spires curve around the Northcove, and each of them leans away from the cove."
good. the spires are the shielding agent, the Northcove is what is shielded, and the north wind rides the 'against' phrase with its own kind and its north modifier both recorded.
good. the thirty lanterns become a counted group held by the Northcove, so 'how many lanterns does the Northcove hold?' answers.

good. adjudicated accept — the position is handed to each lantern through the group rule (a property of a plural's members is never predicated of the group symbol itself), and both 'curving' and 'inner' land on the shore.

mixed: the per-lantern burning rule is fireable and winter is recorded, but 'through winter' is coarsened to a plain 'in winter' time slot — we have no carrier for the spans-the-whole-period sense of 'through', so the parse only says the burning happens at some point in winter. Your own later sentence ('never go out in winter') restores that half; to have it inside this one sentence, write "Northcove lanterns burn in winter, and they never go out in winter."

good. the rule denies the need at zero strength for every Northcove lantern, which is exactly what 'need no salt-bloom' claims; only the surface word 'no' goes unrecorded, and nothing is lost by that here.
good. 'never' lands as a zero-strength per-lantern rule with the quantifier word recorded beside it, and the Northcove link, the 'go out' phrasal verb and the winter slot are all kept.
good. the Northcove is typed as a production-row with its 'row' genus, and 'reliable' stays its own atom rather than being fused into the kind.
The cliff-spires rise above the eastern cliff.
Each cliff-spire is a smooth stone column.
Sea wind weathered the cliff-spires over centuries.
The sky-cats roost on the tops of the cliff-spires.
The cliff-spires are visible from the village.
When sky-cats sit on the cliff-spires in the morning, the day stays calm.

(: whenever_sit_calm (Implication (And (Member $x sky_cat) (Member $e sit) (Experiencer $e $x) (Location $e sk_cliff_spire_1) (Time $e morning)) (And (Member (sk_calm $e) calm) (Member (sk_day $e) day) (Experiencer (sk_calm $e) (sk_day $e)) (Still (sk_calm $e)) (Member (sk_day $e) calm) (During (sk_calm $e) $e))) (STV 0.9 0.9))

good. read as a plain position clause — no invented 'rise' event — with the above-relation handed to each spire through the group rule, and the eastern cliff typed with its positional modifier exposed.
good. nine cliff-spires become a group with an exact count, so 'how many cliff-spires are there?' answers.
good. 'each' distributes both the stone-column kind and the smoothness to cliff-spires, with the column genus recorded and the quantifier word kept beside each claim.
good. the sea wind is the agent, the spires the group that was changed, and 'over centuries' lands as a duration of at least two centuries.

bad: ruled defective — the parse never records that a sky-cat is a cat (the genus atom a fused compound like 'sky-cat' always owes), so nothing said about cats reaches these roosting animals; that half is our slip and a re-parse fixes it. The wording does contribute one real problem of its own: 'the tops of the cliff-spires' yields a part-of link between two whole groups, which never says which top belongs to which spire. Rewrite: "The sky-cats roost on top of the cliff-spires."

bad: ruled defective — the parse builds a per-spire 'visible' state with the from-the-village link but drops the plain half, so a bare 'is that cliff-spire visible?' binds nothing. The sentence itself is not at fault and a re-parse should fix it; if you would rather sidestep the adjective-plus-phrase machinery altogether, write "The cliff-spires can be seen from the village.", which becomes an ordinary seeing event with a can-marker.

mixed: the rule is fireable and the morning sitting, the spires and the stays-calm state all land, but two things drift — the calm is tied to the trigger by a 'during' link that puts the calm inside the morning sitting (the reverse of what you mean, since the calm outlasts it), and 'the day', a definite that changes with every occasion, forces the translator to invent a per-occasion day symbol we have no rule for. Rewrite: "When sky-cats sit on the cliff-spires in the morning, the weather stays calm until evening." — the weather is one standing referent, and 'until evening' gives the calm its own explicit end instead of borrowing the trigger's extent.
The Cold Sea stretches north of the cliffs.
The Cold Sea is grey-green in summer.
The Cold Sea is slate-grey in winter.
The fishing boats stay near the inlet.
The cold-threshold wind comes off the Cold Sea.
good. the Cold Sea keeps its name and its sea kind, the cliffs become a group, and 'north of' is recorded as a direct position link with no invented event for 'stretches'.

mixed: the grey-green state is recorded with its summer time slot, but our copular-with-a-time rule also emits a bare, season-free 'the Cold Sea is grey-green'; set beside your winter sentence, the store then holds both colours unconditionally. No rewording of a plain 'X is ADJ in <season>' avoids that — it is our rule, not your phrasing. If you want only the seasonal reading recorded, make the season a recurring trigger: "Whenever summer comes, the Cold Sea turns grey-green."

mixed: same as the summer line — the slate-grey state carries its winter slot, but the parse also asserts a bare 'the Cold Sea is slate-grey' with no season attached, so the two colour sentences together make the sea both colours at once. Rewrite along the same lines: "Whenever winter comes, the Cold Sea turns slate-grey."

mixed: each boat's nearness to the inlet lands and the rule fires, but 'stay' is flattened to a plain 'is near' — we have no carrier for the keeps-to-it sense of stay/remain with a place, so the standing habit itself is not recorded. If that habit matters, use a verb the translator can reify: "The fishing boats shelter near the inlet."
good. the wind's compound kind and its 'wind' genus both land, 'off the Cold Sea' is recorded as the source of the coming, and the sea keeps its name and its kind.
The village square sits between the harbor and the Watch.
A weekly market runs in the village square.
Boats from down the coast bring grain, salt, cloth, and ironmongery to the market.
The villagers use the market salt for cooking.
Imported salt does not yield mire-essence.
Mire-essence distillation requires sea-water from the local pools.

(: boats_bring_rule (Implication (And (Member $x boat) (From $x sk_coast_1)) (And (Member (sk_bring $x) bring) (Agent (sk_bring $x) $x) (Theme (sk_bring $x) grain) (Theme (sk_bring $x) salt) (Theme (sk_bring $x) cloth) (Theme (sk_bring $x) ironmongery) (Goal (sk_bring $x) sk_market_1))) (STV 0.9 0.9))

mixed: all the content is captured, but 'between A and B' has no supported two-landmark position form, so the parse had to improvise a three-place link that no reasoning rule reaches and that a later re-parse may render differently. If you want the position to be stable and queryable, split it into two ordinary position statements: 'The harbor lies on one side of the village square, and the Watch lies on the other side.'

mixed: the parse is faithful, but 'weekly' sitting inside the noun phrase lands only as a plain property of the market, so nothing records the recurrence and 'how often does the market run?' finds nothing. Move the frequency out of the noun phrase into the clause: 'A market runs in the village square every week.'

bad: the four goods are stacked onto one delivery event, which reads as a single joint shipment of all four rather than four things the boats bring, and there is no supported way to split a coordinated object list inside a generic rule of this shape; 'down' was also dropped, widening the origin to the coast at large. bad: the object stacks a nominalized "hunts" with "sky-cat" as its unstated subject and "of other insects" as its object, a shape we cannot encode, so the parse ended up asserting a free-standing generalization that sky-cats hunt insects, which your sentence only reports the logs as recording; "other" is again uncarriable. The hunting is then held as what the logs say rather than asserted as a fact about sky-cats, and the prey kinds can be named separately if the exclusion matters.

bad: nothing composes a kind subject with a possessed predicate nominal, so "the sky-cats'" never reaches the predication: the parse asserts flatly that nightmoths are main food and hangs the sky-cats off the bare kind "main food", which would make anything else typed that way theirs too. Turn it into a verbal claim with both kinds as arguments: "Sky-cats usually eat nightmoths." That records the sky-cat/nightmoth relation and carries "main" through the frequency reading; the continuation sense of "remain" has no carrier for a kind-level claim and will be lost whatever the wording.
